Capacitor is probably a large can about size of a beer can. It triggers the compressor and the electric motor which turns your fan. Open the system door and look at the capacitor. Write down the various data on it: things like volts, uF (microfarads), and manufacturer name. Doubtful you will find an OEM replacement but you may find a very close replacement. Be absolutely certain you either draw or make a photo of the 4 terminals and wire colors at the end of the capacitor can. When you find the replacement, turn off the 220 volt break to shut down the system. Replace the capacitor by plugging the various colored wires into the EXACT same terminals on the new can. Turn the breaker back on and see if the system starts. Also if the compressor has been working hard you should use your water hose to spray cold water on the compressor for about 5 minutes before re-starting the system. "Jamming" the contactor is a very bad idea as it will cause the compressor to overheat and destroy itself. Thus, instead of a $20 capacitor you will have a $2,000 compressor replacement to pay for. One moar thing, since the system is 20 years old, think about replacing the electric motor which turns the cooling fan as it is likely at the end of its lifespan. Do same data gathering on electric motor as you did with capacitor, go through same measures, unbolt the motor and replace with a one of similar HP and voltage.

for fucks sake, so many responses are wrong. delaying the restart of the compressor is so the high-side pressure has a chance to bleed out into the system. a compressor start sequence is designed to bring up the high side pressure from an idle state, and if it was just running then there is already pressure that must be overcome to spin up to operating speed. The reason for the delay is not due to it being hot, but because the spinup of the compressor is MUCH HARDER if there is already high pressure to overcome. That is one of the reasons why compressors have automatically-resetting overload circuit breakers attached to their casing.
